newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME copper seen soft, Asian metal demand steady.
newsitem.headline: LME copper seen soft, Asian metal demand steady.

text.p: Far East base metal dealers said three-month copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) will probably slip lower later on Tuesday with a test of US$2,200 and then $2,000 seen in the next few weeks.
"Copper should open weak. There's nothing holding it up," one dealer said. "I feel it's going to test $2,200 (a tonne)."
"The copper price still looks soft. I don't see it moving up," the general manager of a Japanese metal trading firm said.
LME copper staged a mini-rally on Monday on shortcovering and bargain-hunting to close the kerb at $2,257, $15 down on the day but off the lows below $2,250.
Three-month LME copper were quoted by the trade at 0330 GMT at $2,259/64 a tonne.
"Prices still failed to close above the 100-day moving average at $2,259 and this leaves the market vulnerable," metal brokers Brandeis said in its daily review.
The copper chart's "medium term uptrend line has been broken and a sloping head and shoulders pattern is developing. Depending on where the neckline is drawn, falls towards $2,000 are indicated."
LME aluminium prices are also seen moving lower.
"Aluminium still looks weak," an aluminium dealer for a Japanese trading house said: "$1,550 is one of the supporting lines, if it breaks through it may go to $1,520 or something."
Brandeis said the market remains "vulnerable to probes towards support at $1,535 and should this fail to hold, crucial support at the $1,500 level."
Three-month aluminium was seen by regional dealers at 0330 GMT at $1,550/55 a tonne against the close in London of $1,549.
Asian base metal demand, particularly for zinc and lead, remained steady but not on the same level seen in the first two months of 1997, dealers said.

"Demand for most of the metals remains steady. It's just coming off the peaks we saw in the first couple of months," a dealer for a European metal trading company said. "A lot of the buyers are stepping back a bit."
Despite the fall in copper prices, there were only bits and pieces of buying seen from the Chinese. "We're not seeing very strong buying from that end," one said.
Most of the trade is virtually ignoring the LME stocks report, which is now released on a daily basis. It used to be issued twice a week on Tuesday and Friday.
"On a daily basis, it's become pointless," one dealer said. "If there is a 5,000 or 4,000 tonne (movement), the market will react. Now, we don't."

Singapore-based dealers don't expect any surprises when the report is released at 0800 GMT. Copper stocks are seen slipping 2,000-3,000 tonnes while aluminium inventories are forecast to fall by 1,000-2,000 tonnes.
